Forge Vertical supports
the AI push for the
Western Cape. Here is what it should actually look like.

The Western Cape already has the highest internet access rate in South Africa at 88.1%. AI is already monitoring 5,000 kilometres of provincial roads. The foundation is there. But government websites still crash. Home Affairs queues still stretch around the block. Permit applications still time out mid-submission. Online systems that are supposed to save people hours instead waste them. Here is Forge Vertical's position on what AI in the Western Cape should actually deliver — and what has to change for it to get there.

Jarrit Hosking
Forge Vertical · Cape Town · September 9, 2026
13 min read
// Where we stand — the honest baseline

Forge Vertical is a Cape Town business. Built here, operating here, serving clients here and globally. When government services work — when a permit application goes through cleanly, when a business registration doesn't require three office visits and a prayer — it saves time that goes back into building things. When they don't work, it costs time that nobody gets back.

That is the position this article comes from. Not political. Not ideological. Practical. AI in the Western Cape is worth supporting because the province has the infrastructure, the connectivity, the startup ecosystem, and the will to actually do something with it — if the implementation is serious rather than cosmetic.

(cite index="20-1">According to the 2023 General Household Survey by StatsSA, at 88.1%, the Western Cape already has the highest internet access rate in the country. That matters. Digital services require digital access. The Western Cape is the one province where a comprehensive online government service strategy can reach the majority of the population it serves.

What is already working — give credit where it is due

// Chapter 01 — The genuine wins

Before getting to what is broken, it is worth being honest about what is working. The Western Cape is genuinely ahead of the rest of the country on several fronts — and those wins deserve acknowledgement because they show what is possible when implementation is taken seriously.

(cite index="19-1">The Western Cape Department of Infrastructure adopted Bentley Systems' AI-powered Blyncsy platform to monitor roughly 5,000 kilometres of roads. The system provides a level of visibility that was previously impossible — a precise digital inventory of assets including guardrails and streetlights, ensuring maintenance crews are deployed where they are needed most. This is AI doing exactly what it should do in government: replacing manual inspection processes that are slow, expensive, and incomplete with continuous automated monitoring that catches problems before they become emergencies.

(cite index="20-1">Liquid Intelligent Technologies and the Western Cape Government renewed their partnership to expand connectivity across the province — an investment of over R2 billion over seven years, adding free public Wi-Fi hotspots and extending high-speed connectivity to government buildings, schools, hospitals, and clinics. Connectivity is infrastructure. The Western Cape is treating it that way.

SARS e-filing works. The Western Cape education ePortal works. These are not small things — they demonstrate that government digital services can be reliable when they are resourced and designed properly.

The GEM Western Cape Report 2026: (cite index="16-1">The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor findings reveal an entrepreneurial ecosystem characterised by high levels of innovation, international ambition, and digital adoption. The Western Cape's startup ecosystem is real, growing, and increasingly international. The province that can connect that private sector energy to public sector digital transformation has a genuine competitive advantage over every other province in the country.

What is broken — the honest list

// Chapter 02 — The problems AI needs to fix

Here is the part that requires honesty. The Western Cape's ambitions for AI-enabled government are real. The gap between those ambitions and the current state of online government services is also real. You cannot leapfrog to AI-powered services when the baseline services are unreliable. You have to fix the foundation first.

// Current reality
Home Affairs queues
Hours-long physical queues for processes that should be completable online. ID applications, passport renewals, birth registrations — all requiring in-person visits to offices that are understaffed and under-resourced. (cite index="15-1">Members of Parliament have raised concerns that Home Affairs systems have never seen proper infrastructure investment and crash regularly — worsened by load shedding.
// What AI can deliver
Digital-first ID and document services
Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber is already pushing digital transformation — AI-powered document verification, online appointment systems that actually hold slots, digital ID issuance that doesn't require a printer and a wet stamp. (cite index="17-1">South Africa is replacing broken bureaucracy with AI-powered digital services, eliminating queues and revolutionising government. The technology exists. Implementation is the gap.
// Current reality
Government websites that crash, time out, and break
Permit applications that time out after 15 minutes of form-filling. E-government portals that return blank pages at the submission step. Online systems that refer you back to the physical office. Systems built on infrastructure so old that load shedding takes them offline entirely. Not hypothetical — documented experience for thousands of Western Cape residents weekly.
// What AI can deliver
Reliable, resilient online application systems
Applications that save progress automatically. Systems that work on mobile as well as desktop. Forms that validate in real time rather than returning generic errors after submission. AI assistants that guide applicants through requirements before they start, reducing rejected applications. Cloud-hosted infrastructure that does not go offline during load shedding. None of this is advanced AI — it is basic modern web development applied to government systems that have not been updated in a decade.
// Current reality
Paperwork duplication and manual processing
The same information submitted to multiple departments separately. Physical documents required for processes that have no legal requirement for paper originals. Manual verification processes that take weeks when automated equivalents take seconds. Business licences, building permits, zoning applications — each carrying its own paper trail that lives in a physical folder in a physical office.
// What AI can deliver
Single-submission, cross-department data sharing
Submit your ID number once. The system pulls your verified information from Home Affairs. You do not retype your address for every department. AI-assisted document processing that reads and verifies uploaded documents in seconds. Digital audit trails that replace physical folders. Automated status updates so you are not calling an office to ask where your application is. The Western Cape e-government framework already has this ambition — it needs the execution to match.

The seven things AI should actually do for Western Cape residents

// Chapter 03 — Specific, practical, achievable

These are not blue-sky predictions. These are applications of existing AI technology to problems that Western Cape residents experience right now. Every one of them is technically feasible today. The question is execution and political will.

  • 01
    AI-assisted permit and licence applications
    An AI that reads your application before you submit it and tells you what is missing, what is wrong, and what supporting documents you still need. Not after rejection — before submission. Cape Town residents submit building permits, business licences, and zoning applications that get rejected weeks later for missing a single document that could have been flagged in seconds. That delay costs money and time that small businesses cannot afford.
  • 02
    24/7 AI government assistant
    A government-built, privacy-respecting AI assistant that can answer "what documents do I need to register a business in Cape Town," "how do I appeal a rates assessment," "what is the process for a rezoning application" — accurately, in plain language, at any hour. Not a FAQ page. A conversational assistant that understands the question and gives the right answer. SARS has demonstrated this works. The Western Cape should replicate it across all service departments.
  • 03
    Predictive maintenance for public infrastructure
    The road monitoring AI is already deployed. The same logic applies to water infrastructure, electricity substations, stormwater drainage, and public buildings. Maintenance that is scheduled based on AI-predicted failure probability is cheaper and less disruptive than emergency repair after the fact. The Western Cape's R27.9 billion infrastructure budget goes further when it is spent proactively rather than reactively.
  • 04
    Court and tribunal scheduling — eliminate the R15,000 lawyer's fee for a date
    The current court scheduling system in South Africa requires, in practice, either a lawyer or extensive patience to navigate. AI-powered scheduling that allows self-represented parties to understand their options, book available dates, and receive preparation guidance would meaningfully improve access to justice for Western Cape residents who cannot afford R15,000 for a consultation that ends with a court date six months away.
  • 05
    Real-time service delivery monitoring
    AI monitoring of service delivery metrics across Cape Town's sub-councils — response times to maintenance requests, water quality readings, electricity outage patterns, refuse collection completion rates. Published publicly. In real time. Not in an annual report that nobody reads — on a dashboard that any resident can open and see whether their sub-council is performing. Accountability through transparency, enabled by AI aggregation of data that already exists but is not being used.
  • 06
    Healthcare triage and appointment routing
    An AI triage system for Western Cape public health facilities that helps patients understand whether their condition requires an emergency room, a clinic visit, or a teleconsultation — and books the appropriate appointment automatically. Reducing ER overcrowding by routing non-emergency cases to the right level of care is one of the highest-impact applications of AI in public health. The Western Cape has the connectivity to make this work at scale.
  • 07
    Business registration and compliance — same day
    Registering a business in the Western Cape currently involves CIPC at national level, the South African Revenue Service, the Department of Labour, and potentially municipal licencing — each with separate systems, separate timelines, and separate requirements. An AI-orchestrated single-submission business registration that coordinates across all four simultaneously, returning a complete registration package within 24 hours, would be transformative for the province's entrepreneurial ecosystem. The GEM 2026 report identifies this as a priority. The technology to deliver it exists today.

The condition — what has to be true for this to work

// Chapter 04 — Forge Vertical's position

AI in government is only as good as the processes it automates. If the underlying process is broken, AI makes it a faster broken process. If the data it draws on is inaccurate, AI gives inaccurate answers with more confidence. If the system it runs on crashes during load shedding, it crashes with a more sophisticated error message.

The condition for AI to actually improve Western Cape government services is that the infrastructure underneath it has to work first. Reliable power at government facilities — which means solar and battery backup, not dependence on Eskom stability. Cloud-hosted systems that do not go offline when the lights go out. Data that is clean, current, and properly maintained. APIs that connect departments rather than silos that talk to nobody.

(cite index="15-1">Members of Parliament raised concerns about the reliability of national government systems — that they crash often and that load shedding makes this worse. They specifically noted that Home Affairs systems have never seen proper infrastructure investment. That is the problem AI cannot solve by itself. The Western Cape government can build the best AI application in Africa — and if it runs on a database that has not been properly backed up since 2019, on a server that goes offline at Stage 4, the application fails.

AI in government is only as good as the processes it automates and the infrastructure it runs on. A sophisticated chatbot that queries a broken database returns sophisticated wrong answers. Fix the foundation first. Build the AI second.

Forge Vertical's position is this: the Western Cape AI push is worth supporting, worth building toward, and worth pushing to happen faster. The province has the connectivity, the ecosystem, and the demonstrated willingness to use technology seriously — the road monitoring AI is proof of that. The gap between ambition and execution in public-facing services is real and needs to be named honestly, because naming it is what drives the investment to close it.

As a Cape Town business that builds digital systems — that has seen firsthand what AI can do when it is implemented properly — we are in a position to say both things at once: this is worth doing, and it has to be done right. The Western Cape can lead South Africa on AI-enabled public services. The question is whether the execution matches the ambition.
